nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, playwright, essayist, music critic and activist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet and playwright, the central theorist and most visible figure of the Black Arts Movement, whose Dutchman and The Dead Lecturer turned the anger of the early 1960s into a poetry of public address and whose later work moved through Black nationalism to Marxism
biography: Amiri Baraka was born Everett LeRoi Jones in Newark, New Jersey, on 7 October 1934, the son of a postal supervisor and a social worker; he grew up in the city's predominantly Black Central Ward, which he would write about for sixty years. He took a BA in English at Howard University in 1954, served in the US Air Force as a meteorologist and gunner from 1954 to 1957 - a period he described as the beginning of his political education, and which ended with a discharge after his annotated copy of Lenin was found - and settled in Greenwich Village, where he co-edited the little magazines Yugen and Kulchur and ran Totem Press, publishing Frank O'Hara, Diane di Prima and Jack Kerouac. Preface to a Twenty Volume Suicide Note (1961) was his first book of poems; Blues People: Negro Music in White America (1963) was the first full-length history of Black music by a Black American writer; The Dead Lecturer (1964) and the plays Dutchman and The Slave (1964) made him, at thirty, the most discussed Black writer in the country. After the assassination of Malcolm X in February 1965 he left Greenwich Village for Harlem, founded the Black Arts Repertory Theatre/School, and published the essays of Home: Social Essays (1966); he took the name Imamu Amiri Baraka in 1967, returned to Newark after the riots of that year, and was arrested and beaten by police during the disturbances, an experience recorded in his play and in his testimony. Black Magic (1969) collected the nationalist poetry; from the early 1970s he moved towards Marxism-Leninism and organised in Newark through the Congress of Afrikan People and later the League of Revolutionary Struggle, writing Hard Facts (1975) and Poetry for the Advanced (1979). He taught at the State University of New York at Stony Brook from 1985 until his retirement in 2013, was appointed New Jersey's second poet laureate in 2002 and held the post for sixteen months before it was abolished, and died in Newark on 9 January 2014.
literary_profile: Poetry: Preface to a Twenty Volume Suicide Note (1961), The Dead Lecturer (1964), Black Art (1966), Black Magic: Sabotage; Target Study; Black Art (1969), It's Nation Time (1970), Spirit Reach (1972), Hard Facts (1975), Poetry for the Advanced (1979), Reggae or Not! (1981), Transbluesency: The Selected Poems 1961-1995 (1995) and Somebody Blew Up America and Other Poems (2003). Drama: Dutchman and The Slave (1964), The Baptism and The Toilet (1966), The Slave Ship (1969), Four Black Revolutionary Plays (1969) and The Motion of History (1978). Prose: Blues People (1963), Home: Social Essays (1966), Black Music (1968), Raise Race Rays Raze (1971), The Autobiography of LeRoi Jones (1984) and Digging: The Afro-American Soul of American Classical Music (2009).
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry built for the voice, with the line broken wherever the breath or the argument breaks; the vernacular and the obscene used as instruments of refusal; the names of the dead spoken aloud; a jazz-derived rhythm that repeats a phrase until it becomes a demand; and, in the later work, the flat declarative sentence of the political pamphlet set inside the lyric.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the refusal of assimilation; the Black artist's obligation to the community; Malcolm X, Newark and the memory of the 1967 rebellion; the relation of Black music - blues, bebop, free jazz - to Black writing; the American state as a machine of violence; and, in the late work, class and empire alongside race.
historical_significance: Baraka is the founder and the most influential figure of the Black Arts Movement, and the writer through whom the American avant-garde of the 1950s became the Black nationalism of the 1960s. Dutchman is a set text and a standing part of the American repertoire; 'Black Art' is the poem most often reprinted to define the movement's aesthetic; Blues People remains the founding work of Black music criticism; and his influence on the poets of the Black Arts generation is acknowledged on every side.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Baraka, the Poetry Foundation's author page, and library catalogue records of The Dead Lecturer and Black Magic; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records four Norton selections - 'An Agony. As Now.', 'A Poem for Willie Best', 'Black Art' and 'Will They Cry When You're Gone, You Bet' - so the other books of poems, the plays, the essays and the music criticism have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; Kiowa novelist, poet, essayist and scholar writing in English
literary_identity: Kiowa American novelist, poet and scholar whose House Made of Dawn won the Pulitzer Prize in 1969 and opened the Native American Renaissance, and whose The Way to Rainy Mountain remade the essay and the poem as instruments of tribal history
biography: Navarre Scott Momaday was born in Lawton, Oklahoma, on 27 February 1934, of Kiowa descent through his father, the painter Al Momaday, and English and Cherokee descent through his mother, Natachee Scott Momaday, a writer and teacher; he spent his childhood on reservations in the Southwest, principally at Jemez Pueblo in New Mexico, and drew on that upbringing in everything he wrote. He took a BA in political science at the University of New Mexico in 1958, an MA and a PhD in English at Stanford, where he studied with Yvor Winters, and taught at the University of California at Santa Barbara, Berkeley, Stanford and, from 1982, the University of Arizona, where he was Regents Professor of English and founded the poetry centre that now bears his name. House Made of Dawn (1968), his first novel, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1969 and is generally taken as the beginning of the Native American Renaissance; The Way to Rainy Mountain (1969), illustrated by his father, retraced the Kiowa migration from the Yellowstone headwaters to the Wichita Mountains through legend, historical commentary and memoir. Angle of Geese and Other Poems (1974), The Gourd Dancer (1976), The Names: A Memoir (1976), The Ancient Child (1989), In the Presence of the Sun (1992) and The Man Made of Words (1997) followed. He was awarded the National Medal of Arts in 2007 and a Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 2024 for the posthumous collection The Earth in Our Hands, delivered the first Native American inaugural benediction in 2021, and died in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on 24 January 2024.
literary_profile: Fiction: House Made of Dawn (1968), The Ancient Child (1989) and the children's book Circle of Wonder (1994). Poetry: Angle of Geese and Other Poems (1974), The Gourd Dancer (1976), In the Presence of the Sun: Stories and Poems 1961-1991 (1992), Again the Far Morning: New and Selected Poems (2011) and The Earth in Our Hands (2024). Prose: The Journey of Tai-me (1967), The Way to Rainy Mountain (1969), The Names: A Memoir (1976), The Man Made of Words (1997) and Three Plays (2007).
stylistic_characteristics: A prose that moves between three registers without warning - the oracular, the documentary and the anecdotal - and sets them side by side rather than blending them; a syntax that takes the cadence of oral narrative and slows it to the pace of writing; the landscape as a participant rather than a setting; and a habit of ending a passage on a sentence that sounds like a proverb without being one.
intellectual_concerns: The land and the memory of a people's migration; the oral tradition as a form of history; the relation of the individual to the tribe and of the tribe to the American state; the Kiowa and Jemez sacred landscape of Oklahoma and New Mexico; loss, survival and the continuity of language; and the act of bearing witness as the writer's office.
historical_significance: Momaday is the founding figure of the Native American Renaissance and the writer most responsible for the presence of Native American literature in the American canon. House Made of Dawn's Pulitzer Prize in 1969 is the event that criticism dates the beginning of that renaissance from, The Way to Rainy Mountain is a standard text in courses on American autobiography and on the essay, and his 2024 Pulitzer for poetry made him one of the few writers honoured in two genres by that prize.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Momaday and from the bibliographic record of The Way to Rainy Mountain; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records two Norton selections - 'Headwaters' and the selections from The Way to Rainy Mountain, which share one record - so the novels, the other poems and the plays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet, the best-selling poet in the United States in the last quarter of the twentieth century, whose close attention to the ordinary natural world - the grasshopper, the pond, the owl - made a devotional poetry of observation that a mass readership took to its own
biography: Mary Jane Oliver was born in Maple Heights, Ohio, on 10 September 1935 and grew up in a house she later described as unhappy; she began writing poems at fourteen, and at seventeen visited Edna St. Vincent Millay's house in Austerlitz, New York, and stayed to help the family sort Millay's papers, a stay that she said decided her life. She attended Ohio State University and Vassar College without taking a degree, moved to Provincetown, Massachusetts, in the late 1950s, and lived there for the rest of her life with the photographer Molly Malone Cook, running a small bookshop and later working as an editor at the Provincetown house of the publisher Houghton Mifflin. No Voyage and Other Poems (1963) was her first book; she published it at twenty-eight. She wrote at first in the formal metres she had learned from Millay and from her reading of the English Romantics, then, from the late 1960s, in a stripped free verse of short lines and single images. American Primitive (1983) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry; New and Selected Poems (1992) won the National Book Award; House of Light (1990), from which 'The Summer Day' comes, won the Christopher Award and the L. L. Winship/PEN New England Award; Why I Wake Early (2004), Thirst (2006), Evidence (2009), Swan (2010), A Thousand Mornings (2012), Dog Songs (2013), Blue Horses (2014) and Felicity (2015) followed. She gave very few interviews and readings and refused most public appearances, and died at her home in Hobe Sound, Florida, on 17 January 2019.
literary_profile: Poetry: No Voyage and Other Poems (1963), The River Styx, Ohio and Other Poems (1972), The Night Traveler (1978), Sleeping in the Forest (1979), Twelve Moons (1979), American Primitive (1983), Dream Work (1986), Provincetown (1987), House of Light (1990), New and Selected Poems (1992), White Pine (1994), West Wind (1997), The Leaf and the Cloud (2000), What Do We Know (2002), Owls and Other Fantasies (2003), Why I Wake Early (2004), Blue Iris (2004), Thirst (2006), Red Bird (2008), Evidence (2009), Swan (2010), A Thousand Mornings (2012), Dog Songs (2013), Blue Horses (2014), Felicity (2015) and Devotions (2017). Prose: A Poetry Handbook (1994), Rules for the Dance (1998), Winter Hours (1999), Long Life (2004) and Upstream (2016).
stylistic_characteristics: Short free-verse lines, often unpunctuated or lightly punctuated, each carrying one image; a repeated question addressed to the world rather than to a person; a vocabulary of ordinary things - grass, pond, heron, blackberries - used without ornament; and an ending that turns the observation into a direct address to the reader, which is the move her critics hold against her and her readers love her for.
intellectual_concerns: Attention as a discipline and a form of praise; the natural world as a place where the sacred is available without doctrine; mortality, and the ordinary fact of being alive in a body; solitude, walking and the deliberate narrowness of a life; and, in the later books, grief, and the death of the companion she lived with for forty years.
historical_significance: Oliver is the most widely read American poet of the last forty years and the one whose work has done most to keep a general readership for poetry in the United States: New and Selected Poems sold more than a million copies, and 'The Summer Day', with its closing question about 'your one wild and precious life', is among the most quoted American poems of the period. Her Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award make her the most decorated popular poet of her generation; academic criticism has been slower than the public, and the argument about her is now a standard part of the discussion of American poetry's readership.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Oliver and the Poetry Foundation's author page; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'The Summer Day' - so the twenty-odd other collections, the essays and the handbooks have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, memoirist and children's writer writing in English
literary_identity: American poet whose short, unpunctuated, lower-case poems of family, body and history made a vernacular lyric of Black American womanhood, and whose eleven collections and twenty-one children's books carried that voice to a readership far beyond the poetry world
biography: Lucille Clifton was born Thelma Lucille Sayles in Depew, New York, on 27 June 1936, the daughter of a steelworker and a laundress, and grew up in Buffalo; she was the first person in her family to finish high school, took a scholarship to Howard University in 1953, and left after two years for Fredonia State Teachers College, where she acted in a production of a play by the poet Ishmael Reed, who became a friend and sent her poems to Langston Hughes. She married Fred Clifton, a philosophy teacher and sculptor, in 1959, and they had six children; his death in 1984 is the subject of much of her later work. Her first collection, Good Times (1969), was chosen by The New York Times as one of the ten best books of the year, and she published it while raising the children and working as a clerk and as a literature assistant at the US Department of Education. Good News About the Earth (1972), An Ordinary Woman (1974), Two-Headed Woman (1980, the Juniper Prize), Next (1987), Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (1991), The Book of Light (1993), The Terrible Stories (1996), Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems 1988-2000 (2000, the National Book Award), Mercy (2004) and Voices (2008) followed. She taught at Columbia, George Washington University and St. Mary's College of Maryland, served as poet laureate of Maryland from 1979 to 1985, read at the first and second inaugurations of Bill Clinton, and died in Baltimore on 13 February 2010.
literary_profile: Poetry: Good Times (1969), Good News About the Earth (1972), An Ordinary Woman (1974), Two-Headed Woman (1980), Next (1987), Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (1991), The Book of Light (1993), The Terrible Stories (1996), Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems 1988-2000 (2000), Mercy (2004) and Voices (2008); collected in The Collected Poems of Lucille Clifton 1965-2010 (2012). Memoir: Generations (1976). Children's books: twenty-one titles, including the Everett Anderson series (1970-1983) and The Lucky Stone (1979).
stylistic_characteristics: Very short free-verse poems in lower case, without punctuation, so that a line break does the work a comma would do; a plain vocabulary and a syntax close to speech; the single image held for a whole poem; a repeated name or phrase as a refrain; and an ending that is usually a flat declarative sentence, which is where the poem's emotional weight lands.
intellectual_concerns: Family and ancestry, especially the mother and the Dahomey women she claimed as forebears; the Black female body, its appetites and its changes; motherhood and the loss of children; death, and the deaths of her husband and her parents; the Black American past, from slavery to the civil rights movement; and the ordinary dignity of people the society has set aside.
historical_significance: Clifton is one of the central American poets of the postwar period and the one whose formal economy did most to show that a poem of twenty short lines could carry a history. Blessing the Boats won the National Book Award in 2000, she held the Maryland laureateship for six years, and her influence runs through the Black Arts and feminist poetry of the 1970s into the work of the poets who came after; 'homage to my hips' and 'miss rosie' are among the most anthologised American poems of the period.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Clifton, the EBSCO and Poetry Foundation author pages, and catalogue records of Good Times, Two-Headed Woman and Quilting; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records seven Norton selections - 'miss rosie', 'the lost baby poem', 'homage to my hips', 'wishes for sons', 'blessing the boats', 'to my last period' and 'wild blessings' - so the other collections, the memoir and the twenty-one children's books have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, short-story writer and playwright writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist of the systems novel, whose White Noise, Libra and Underworld made the media, the conspiracy and the American century itself into the matter of literary fiction
biography: Don DeLillo was born in New York City on 20 November 1936, the son of Italian immigrants from Molise, and grew up in the Bronx; he has said that he did not read a book until he was eighteen. He took a degree in communication arts at Fordham University in 1958, worked for five years in advertising in Manhattan, and began writing fiction in the evenings. Americana (1971) was his first novel; End Zone (1972), Great Jones Street (1973), Ratner's Star (1976) and Players (1977) followed before The Names (1982) and White Noise (1985), which won the National Book Award and made him famous at forty-eight. Libra (1988), a novel of the Kennedy assassination, Mao II (1991), Underworld (1997) - which sold more than any of his other books and is a history of the Cold War told through the baseball that ended the 1951 National League pennant - and The Body Artist (2001), Cosmopolis (2003), Falling Man (2007), Point Omega (2010) and Zero K (2016) followed. He wrote plays - The Engineer of Moonlight (1979), Valparaiso (1999) and Love-Lies-Bleeding (2005) - and essays collected in The Vondelpark (2020). He received the Jerusalem Prize in 1999, the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction in 2013 and the National Book Foundation's Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters in 2014, and died in New York on 13 October 2026.
literary_profile: Novels: Americana (1971), End Zone (1972), Great Jones Street (1973), Ratner's Star (1976), Players (1977), Running Dog (1978), Amazons (1980, as Cleo Birdwell), The Names (1982), White Noise (1985), Libra (1988), Mao II (1991), Underworld (1997), The Body Artist (2001), Cosmopolis (2003), Falling Man (2007), Point Omega (2010), Zero K (2016) and The Silence (2020). Plays: The Engineer of Moonlight (1979), Valparaiso (1999) and Love-Lies-Bleeding (2005). Stories and essays: The Angel Esmeralda (2011) and The Vondelpark (2020).
stylistic_characteristics: Long, flat, declarative sentences that report the most extreme events in the tone of a news wire; dialogue that is mostly people repeating the language of advertising, television and the corporation; lists and catalogues used as a formal device; a narrator who knows more than any character but refuses to explain; and an ending that stops rather than resolves.
intellectual_concerns: Consumer culture and the saturation of daily life by media; the conspiracy as a structure of American history; the fear of death and the technologies that manage it; the family as a site of improvisation and error; the Cold War and its aftermath; and language itself, which his novels treat as a system with its own momentum.
historical_significance: DeLillo is the most influential American novelist of the post-1970 period. White Noise's National Book Award in 1985 is often taken as the moment the academy recognised the novel of media saturation; Underworld was voted one of the great American novels of the century; and his influence runs through the fiction of David Foster Wallace, Jonathan Franzen, Bret Easton Ellis and Jennifer Egan. The Library of America began issuing his work in 2022.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on DeLillo and from the publisher's records of White Noise; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - the 'Airborne Toxic Event' section of White Noise - so the other seventeen novels, the plays and the stories have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

birthplace: Glen Cove, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist, the great recluse of postwar American letters, whose V., Gravity's Rainbow and Mason and Dixon made the historical conspiracy the form of the American novel and who has been fugitive from the public since the 1960s
biography: Thomas Ruggles Pynchon Jr. was born in Glen Cove, New York, on 8 May 1937 and grew up in Long Island; he took a degree in English at Cornell in 1959, where he is said to have attended Vladimir Nabokov's lectures, and served two years in the US Navy before working for the Boeing Company in Seattle, where he wrote technical copy and, in his spare time, his first novel. V. (1963) won the William Faulkner Foundation Award for a first novel; The Crying of Lot 49 (1966) was written while he was living in California; Gravity's Rainbow (1973), a novel of the V-2 rocket and the last months of the Second World War, won the National Book Award in 1974 and was famously awarded the Pulitzer Prize by its fiction jury only to be overruled by the Pulitzer board. Slow Learner (1984) collected his early stories with an introduction that is one of the few autobiographical documents he has published; Vineland (1990), Mason and Dixon (1997), Against the Day (2006), Inherent Vice (2009), Bleeding Edge (2013) and the posthumous Shadow Ticket (2025) followed. He has never given a public reading, has rarely been photographed since the 1960s, and his whereabouts - long rumoured to be New York City - are a running joke in American letters.
literary_profile: Novels: V. (1963), The Crying of Lot 49 (1966), Gravity's Rainbow (1973), Vineland (1990), Mason and Dixon (1997), Against the Day (2006), Inherent Vice (2009), Bleeding Edge (2013) and Shadow Ticket (2025). Stories: Slow Learner (1984), collecting 'The Small Rain' (1959), 'Low-Lands' (1960), 'Entropy' (1960), 'Under the Rose' (1961) and 'The Secret Integration' (1964). Essays: The introduction to Slow Learner (1984) and the collected occasional pieces.
stylistic_characteristics: Sentences that run for pages and subordinate clause upon clause until the reader is lost in the syntax on purpose; an encyclopaedic range of registers, from the bureaucratic to the slapstick; songs, parodies and doggerel set inside the narrative; a plot that is a conspiracy the reader can never fully assemble; and an ending that withholds the revelation it has been promising.
intellectual_concerns: The Second World War and the machinery of the V-2 as an image of the modern state; entropy and the second law of thermodynamics as a metaphor of culture; the underground, the postal system and the counter-histories that official history suppresses; empire and the survey as forms of violence; paranoia as a method of knowledge; and the possibility that the conspiracy is real and knowing it changes nothing.
historical_significance: Pynchon is the central American novelist of the encyclopaedic mode and the one whose work did most to make the postwar American novel a system rather than a story. Gravity's Rainbow is on every short list of the great American novels of the century, the National Book Award of 1974 is only the most official of his honours, and his influence is visible in DeLillo, Wallace, Vollmann and the whole of the literary novel after 1973.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Pynchon and from the record of Slow Learner; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'Entropy' - so the nine novels and the other stories have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer and poet writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and poet, the central figure of the American revival of the story in the 1970s and 1980s, whose spare, unconsoling stories of ordinary people in the American Northwest were first called 'minimalist' and are now simply the sound of the form
biography: Raymond Clevie Carver Jr. was born in Clatskanie, Oregon, on 25 May 1938, the son of a sawmill worker and a waitress, and grew up in Yakima, Washington. He married at nineteen, had two children by twenty-one, and worked - as a delivery boy, a janitor, a farm hand and a sawmill hand - while attending night classes; he took a BA at Chico State in 1963 and an MFA at the University of Iowa in 1965, and taught at several universities for the rest of his life. He was an alcoholic until he stopped drinking in 1977, a fact central to everything he wrote. Will You Please Be Quiet, Please? (1976) was a finalist for the National Book Award; Furious Seasons (1977), What We Talk About When We Talk About Love (1981) and Cathedral (1983) followed, the last two edited by Gordon Lish, whose cuts were so severe that the publication of the manuscripts as Carver wrote them - in 2009 and 2015 - has changed the received account of his style. He also published six books of poems, including Near Klamath (1968), Winter Insomnia (1970), At Night the Salmon Move (1976), Where Water Comes Together with Other Water (1985) and Ultramarine (1986). He was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Letters in 1988, and died of lung cancer in Port Angeles, Washington, on 2 August 1988.
literary_profile: Stories: Will You Please Be Quiet, Please? (1976), Furious Seasons (1977), What We Talk About When We Talk About Love (1981), Cathedral (1983), Elephant (1988) and Call If You Need Me (2000); collected in Where I'm Calling From (1988) and Carver: Collected Stories (Library of America, 2009). Poetry: Near Klamath (1968), Winter Insomnia (1970), At Night the Salmon Move (1976), Where Water Comes Together with Other Water (1985), Ultramarine (1986), A New Path to the Waterfall (1989) and All of Us (1996).
stylistic_characteristics: Short sentences, plain diction and almost no metaphor; dialogue recorded without commentary; detail used sparingly and where it lands hardest; scenes that end before the emotional consequence arrives; and a narrator who reports without judging, which is what gives the stories their pressure.
intellectual_concerns: Drinking and its aftermath; marriage and the slow work of its failure; work and money in the American Northwest; the ordinary epiphany that arrives too late to be useful; class, and the shame of not having enough; and, in the late stories, the possibility of grace.
historical_significance: Carver is the most imitated American short-story writer of the last forty years and the one whose name is attached to the revival of the form in the 1980s. Cathedral was nominated for the National Book Critics Circle Award and the Pulitzer Prize, his stories are in every American anthology of the period, and the publication of his unedited manuscripts has made him a central case in the discussion of what an editor does to a writer.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Carver and from the records of Cathedral; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'Cathedral' - so the other five collections and the six books of poems have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer, novelist, essayist and filmmaker writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and essayist of the Black Arts generation, whose Gorilla, My Love and The Salt Eaters made the speech of Black neighbourhoods into a literary form and whose anthology The Black Woman put Black feminism on the map of American publishing
biography: Toni Cade Bambara was born Miltona Mirkin Cade in New York City on 25 March 1939 and grew up in Harlem, Brooklyn and Queens; she took the name Toni Cade in her teens and added Bambara in 1970 after discovering the West African ethnic group in a friend's artwork. She took a BA in theatre arts at Queens College in 1959, studied mime in Florence, and completed an MA in African American literature at the City College of New York in 1964, with a thesis on the Black short story. She taught at City College and at Livingston College, worked as a community organiser in Newark and New York, and in 1970 edited The Black Woman: An Anthology, one of the first collections of Black feminist writing in the United States. Gorilla, My Love (1972) collected her short stories; The Sea Birds Are Still Alive (1977) followed. The Salt Eaters (1980), her only novel, won the American Book Award and is one of the formal achievements of Black feminist fiction. From the late 1970s she worked increasingly in film, writing the screenplays for The Bombing of Osage Avenue, on the 1985 police bombing of the MOVE house in Philadelphia, and for Louis Massiah's W.E.B. Du Bois: A Biography in Four Voices. She taught at Spelman College and at Rutgers, and died of colon cancer in New York on 9 December 1995; Deep Sightings and Rescue Missions, a posthumous collection of essays and stories, appeared in 1996.
literary_profile: Fiction: Gorilla, My Love (1972), The Sea Birds Are Still Alive (1977) and The Salt Eaters (1980). Anthology and essays: The Black Woman: An Anthology (1970) and Deep Sightings and Rescue Missions (1996). Screenplays: The Bombing of Osage Avenue and W.E.B. Du Bois: A Biography in Four Voices (1996).
stylistic_characteristics: Narration in a child's or a neighbourhood voice that is allowed its own grammar; dialogue in unreconstructed Black vernacular, with the spelling to match; comedy used as a mode of political argument; an ending that withholds the adult's explanation; and a narrative that refuses to translate its community for an outside reader.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the education of a Black girl in the city; the church, the school and the neighbourhood as institutions of both belonging and constraint; the Black Arts and Black feminist politics of the 1970s; class and the economics of survival; and the ordinary genius of people who are not written about.
historical_significance: Bambara is a central figure of the Black Arts Movement and one of the founders of Black feminist literary culture in the United States. The Black Woman was the first anthology of its kind, Gorilla, My Love is a standard text in American fiction courses, and The Salt Eaters is discussed as a landmark of Black feminist experimentation. Her influence on the short story of the 1980s and 1990s is acknowledged by writers from Toni Morrison to Edwidge Danticat.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Bambara and from the catalogue records of Gorilla, My Love; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'The Lesson' - so the novel, the other stories and the anthologies have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.
